We hold that the Veterans Court applied the correct legal standard.
12388: Whether a TDIU claim is a separate claim or part of the underlying increased-rating claim; court held TDIU is part of the rating claim, so the 2013 withdrawal of the rating claim finally resolved the TDIU claim (VA's reading).
In the absence of bifurcation, the issue of TDIU remains part of a veteran's claim for an increased rating.
12472: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 20.1403 CUE standard: whether CUE requires that correcting the error would have changed the ultimate service-connection outcome; court adopted the VA's reading that an error leading only to continued litigation with an uncertain result is insufficient

We agree with the Secretary. For the reasons more fully set forth, infra, the “manifestly different” outcome standard of 38 C.F.R. § 20.1403 cannot be met by correcting an error that leads only to continued litigation with an uncertain result on the merits of the claim.
12647: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. § 3562 nonduplication bar: whether section 3562(2) bars a disabled veteran from receiving additional compensation under § 1115(1)(F) once the child begins receiving DEA benefits; court adopted VA's reading.

We conclude that the nonduplication provision of section 3562 bars a disabled veteran from receiving additional compensation under section 1115(1)(F) once his or her child elects to receive DEA benefits.
12648: Whether the section 3562 bar is permanent or lifts upon exhaustion of DEA benefits; court held the bar is permanent, adopting VA's reading.
The statute clearly imposes a permanent bar on a veteran's receipt of additional compensation under section 1115(1)(F) once his or her child begins to receive DEA benefits.
12649: Application of pro-veteran canon: court found section 3562 unambiguous and declined to apply the canon in the veteran's favor.

we have determined, based on the statutory text and context of section 3562, that the statute imposes on a veteran a permanent bar to additional compensation under section 1115(1)(F) and is not ambiguous.
12727: Whether the Veterans Court misinterpreted 38 C.F.R. § 4.20 (rating by analogy) in reviewing a CUE claim on GERD rated under hiatal hernia DC 7346; court held no misinterpretation.
Because the Veterans Court did not misinterpret 38 C.F.R. § 4.20, we affirm.
12776: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. § 5904(d)(3): whether the 'date of the final decision' limiting attorney fees from past-due benefits is the agency decision date (March 2, 2019) or the notice date (April 26, 2019).

We reject Mr. Dojaquez’s interpretation of § 5904(d)(3) and hold that the end date for the past-due benefits calculation under § 5904(d)(1) and Snyder is also “the date of the final decision” referenced in § 5904(d)(3)’s second sentence.
12848: Interpretation of 10 U.S.C. 1174(h)(2) and 1174a: whether VA recoupment from disability compensation applies to special separation benefit payments; court held the statute requires deduction of SSB payments.

We hold that 10 U.S.C. § 1174(h)(2) applies to benefits received under 10 U.S.C. § 1174a and that separation pay received under 10 U.S.C. § 1174a shall be deducted from VA disability compensation per the requirements of 10 U.S.C. § 1174(h)(2).
12863: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. 1114(r): the court held a veteran qualifies for the 1114(r)(2) aid-and-attendance rate only if he first qualifies for a predicate SMC rate, regardless of required level of care, adopting the VA's reading.

The statute's plain language establishes that a veteran qualifies for the § 1114(r)(2) rate only if he first qualifies for a predicate special monthly compensation rate, regardless of his necessary level of care.
12950: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. 1114 and the SMC framework: the effective date of an SMC award is a separate, downstream issue from entitlement to SMC, so the Board need not decide it, adopting the VA's reading.
the Veterans Court correctly ruled that the question of the effective date of an SMC award is a separate and downstream issue from whether the veteran meets the criteria to qualify for that award.
13010: Application of the pyramiding rule in 38 C.F.R. § 4.14 to bar an additional rating under DC 5259 for the same pain and swelling already rated under DC 5003; the court did not decide the meaning of DC 5003's objective-evidence requirement.
Providing him any further compensation based on that same left knee pain or swelling would constitute improper pyramiding.
13019: Whether the Board and Veterans Court applied an incorrect legal standard for claim scope (Clemons 'reasonable expectations' versus Boggs 'distinct factual bases'); court found no legal error, adopting the VA's reading.
Accordingly, we see no legal error in the standards used to determine claim scope.
13020: Whether the Veterans Court legally erred by disregarding the Board's conclusion that 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c) applied; court held § 3.156(c) requires reconsideration, not favorable decision, and no legal error occurred.
Section 3.156(c) sets forth the circumstances under which the VA must reconsider a claim; it does not mandate the claim be decided favorably upon reconsideration.
13066: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1) and 38 C.F.R. § 3.400(b)(2)(i): whether an effective date can be based on a discharge that was dishonorable (service period ending in dishonorable discharge cannot support earlier effective date).
We hold that the Veterans Court's interpretation of 38 U.S.C. § 5110 and 38 C.F.R. § 3.400 was not arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.
13134: Whether VA had statutory authority under 38 U.S.C. 1720G(a)(3) to set caregiver stipends using the GS scale rather than BLS wage tables; court held stare decisis from Veteran Warriors binds it.
Thus, our previous determination that the VA did not exceed its statutory authority in setting stipend amounts in the July 2020 final rule stands, and binds us to the same conclusion in this case.
13135: Whether 38 U.S.C. 1720G(a)(9)(C) permits in-home reassessment visits; court held 'may include' gives VA discretion and does not let participants opt out.
Contrary to the Lathams' argument, the statute's 'may include' language gives discretion to the VA; it does not empower PCAFC beneficiaries to opt out of home visits.
13136: Whether the rule's in-State residency requirement exceeds VA's statutory authority under 1720G(a); court held it was already determined not to be outside authority.
In Veteran Warriors, 29 F.4th at 1343, we already determined that imposition of the residency requirement was not outside the VA's authority under the statute.
13137: Whether the rule's ADL-centered eligibility framework rewrites 38 U.S.C. 1720G(a)(2)(C)(i) by excluding IADLs; court held the rule mirrors the statute.
Thus, the final rule, which refers to ADLs and not IADLs, mirrors the statutory language and does not rewrite it.
13216: Meaning of 38 U.S.C. 5904(c)(1) phrase 'with respect to the case' for attorney fee eligibility; court adopted VA's reading (new claim for increased rating is a separate case under evidence-focused test)

We agree with the Veterans Court's reasoning and conclude that 'case' in § 5904(c)(1) means all the potential claims that could be raised by the evidence before the VA during the processing of the claim in question.
13217: Whether a September 2021 claim qualified as an AMA supplemental claim under 38 U.S.C. 101(36) and 5108; court held it was not filed under section 5108 and so not a supplemental claim

The problem is that Ms. Jackson neglects that the AMA requires that supplemental claims not only meet the definition in § 101(36), but also that they be filed 'under' § 5108 pursuant to 38 U.S.C. § 5104C(a)(1)(B), (b).
13448: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. 3672(b)(2)(A)(ii) and 3680A(b): whether FAA-approved flight training at a certified pilot school is exempt from the IHL requirement; court adopted the Secretary's reading.

Under Section 3672(b)(2)(A)(ii), FAA-approved courses at certified pilot schools are deemed approved. But the receipt of benefits is subject to Section 3680A(b)'s further requirement that any flight training course be given by an IHL and count toward a veteran's college degree.
13610: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. 3.156(c): reconsideration applies only after VA issues a decision on a claim, so it did not apply to the PTSD and migraine claims
the Veterans Court's legal interpretation is consistent with the language of the regulation.
13618: Whether the Appeals Modernization Act requires the Board member who conducts a hearing to also issue the final determination, and whether 38 U.S.C. § 7102 supplies a same-member requirement; court adopted the VA's reading of the statute.
The statutory scheme and its history are clear—the same judge is not required to both conduct the hearing and author the final determination under the AMA.
13635: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b): court held the Veterans Court did not misinterpret the regulation, so VA's reading (no required new-and-material determination beyond what the Board made) prevails.
We see no error of law in the Veterans Court's decision.
13679: Whether 38 C.F.R. § 20.1400(b)(1) bars a CUE motion to revise a Board order already affirmed by the Veterans Court, and whether 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(a) or 38 U.S.C. § 5108 creates an exception.
Nothing in either 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(a) or 38 U.S.C. § 5108 alters 38 C.F.R. § 20.1400(b)(1)’s bar on seeking revision of a Board order when that order has been affirmed by the Veterans Court.
13680: Whether a Board remand order is a final Board decision subject to CUE revision under 38 C.F.R. § 20.1400(b) (headache claim).
We agree with the Veterans Court. See Howard v. Gober, 220 F.3d 1341, 1344 (Fed. Cir. 2000) (“[T]he Board’s remand does not constitute a final decision that may be appealed.”).
13887: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c), including whether a record in the claims file but overlooked counts as associated with the claims file
We thus reject the interpretation of § 3.156(c) that Ms. Harris urges: that the regulation applies when a record is in the claims file, but is overlooked, or "missed," by the RO.
13982: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.343(a) and 3.344(a): the court accepted the VA's reading of the rating-reduction regulations, as reflected in Collier v. Derwinski, that a reduction may rest on sustained material improvement shown across the entire medical record, rejecting the claimant's two-showing reading.
Thus, the relevant inquiry here is whether the Board misinterpreted the requirements for reducing a total disability rating based on how the disputed regulations were understood in April 2006.
14025: Under the AMA, the VA's 2021 decision that addressed only service connection could not implicitly deny the veteran's request to reopen his character-of-discharge determination; the court construed 38 U.S.C. 5104(b) to require explicit notice of issues adjudicated, so an appealable decision requires explicit notice.
We hold that under the AMA, a veteran's claims can no longer be implicitly denied.
14257: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. §§ 3.105(e) and 3.344(a): whether the RO's failure to make the required findings rendered its rating reduction void ab initio, or whether the Board's subsequent findings cure the deficiency. Court held the Board's findings cured it, so the reduction stands.
In short, neither Brown nor Stern held that the Board's findings cannot cure a deficiency in an RO decision.
14306: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.816: court held federal law required equal distribution of Nehmer accrued benefits among the four children, consistent with VA's reading.
Federal law thus required the VA to distribute the funds to Goldman's four children in equal shares under 38 C.F.R. § 3.816(f) and the VA complied with that law.
14356: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.151(a): whether VA must treat a pension application also as a claim for compensation; court held VA has discretion (may, not must).
The VA may, but is not required to, consider a claim for pension to also include a claim for compensation, and vice versa.
14362: Whether 38 U.S.C. § 7331 (informed consent duty) is a statutory precondition to enforcing the effective-date limits of 38 U.S.C. § 5110; court held it is not, adopting VA's reading.
For these reasons, we conclude 38 U.S.C. § 7331 is not a statutory precondition to the enforcement of 38 U.S.C. § 5110.
14431: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. § 1111: whether an asymptomatic condition noted at service entry can be a preexisting defect that rebuts the presumption of soundness. Court affirmed the Veterans Court's (VA-favored) reading.
We see no error in the Veterans Court’s interpretation that an asymptomatic condition can be noted as a preexisting defect under § 1111.
14447: Interpretation of benefit statutes: whether violation of § 4131 informed consent requirement amounted to a compensable negligence claim under § 351 (1976), read as VA's reading.

The two statutes therefore do not suggest, let alone undebatably so, that the VA's failure to adhere to § 4131's requirement of obtaining a patient's informed consent amounts to a compensable negligence claim under § 351.
14721: Meaning of 'case' in 38 U.S.C. § 5904(c)(1) (2012) for attorney fee eligibility; court held the Veterans Court properly applied Jackson's broad construction, so PTSD claim fees were not allowed.
We likewise agree and see no reason to depart from our prior interpretation given the similarities between the 2006 version of § 5904(c)(1) and its predecessor.
14886: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c)(2) (2006): the event that triggers application of the new regulation is VA's receipt or association of new and relevant service department records, rejecting both the veteran's original-claim trigger and the government's claim-to-reopen trigger.
we hold that the action that invokes the application of the new regulation is the VA's receipt or association of new and relevant service department records.
14942: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 14.636: whether the presumption of reasonableness applies to a fee where the attorney was discharged or withdrew before benefits were awarded; the court held no presumption applies and a reasonableness determination was required.
By the clear language of the regulation, no presumption of reasonableness applies in a case where an attorney withdraws or is discharged before an award of benefits.
14948: Interpretation of 38 U.S.C. §§ 5121 and 5121A: the court rejected the claimant's reading that substitution under §5121A allows recovery of all accrued benefits, holding recovery is limited to the expenses of last sickness and burial under §5121(a)(6).
We reject Mr. Smith's reading of § 5121A.
14994: Interpretation of the PACT Act: whether the Act automatically reopens previously denied claims that are later established as presumptively service connected; the court held it does not and that the Secretary's duties are only to identify claimants and inform them they may file a supplemental claim.
Ms. Robinson's interpretation of the PACT Act is both unsupported by and inconsistent with the statutory text.
15116: Whether pain must be rated as a separate disability under Saunders v. Wilkie and whether double-counting pain is barred by 38 C.F.R. 4.14; court found no legal error in VA's reading
we see no error in the legal assertion that, on this record, there is no legal entitlement, under Saunders or otherwise, to double-counting pain for compensation purposes.
15133: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b): whether a VA delay in addressing new and material evidence submitted during a prior claim's appeal period keeps the prior claim open and entitles the claimant to its earlier application date. The court adopted the VA's reading.
15140: Whether the Board may consider evidence beyond service department records, such as witness testimony, to establish active-duty service classification under 38 C.F.R. § 3.203(a)(1). The court adopted the VA's reading that only service department documentation may establish service classification.
the Board may only consider documentation issued by the relevant service department as evidence to establish a particular service classification.
15252: Whether the Board may find a final VA denial of a nervous-condition claim where the record lacks a notice of decision; claimant's asserted legal rule rejected, so the court found no legal error.
We see no ground for that asserted legal rule.
15253: Whether an explicitly raised claim can be finally denied only by an explicit denial compliant with 38 C.F.R. § 3.103; court held implicit denial is legally permissible under established precedent.
Ms. Carey's second contention, to the extent that it is an assertion of legal error, is fundamentally inconsistent with our established precedent recognizing implicit denials.
15283: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.344 and DC 7528: whether the § 3.344 stabilization procedures apply to rating reductions under DC 7528; court held they do not, adopting the VA's reading as in Foster.
Because we see no legal error in the Veterans Court's analysis, we decline to do so.
15302: Interpretation of 38 C.F.R. 4.71a (Note 1) and 4.25(b): the court held these regulations require neurological abnormalities associated with spine disorders to be rated separately, rejecting the veteran's reading that radiculopathy is merely a symptom of spondylolisthesis.
Instead, the regulations establish that neurological abnormalities associated with diseases or injuries of the spine should be treated as separately rated conditions.
